skeleton:
Bubble and Squeak

British · Easy · Serves 4 as a breakfast component

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The great Monday-morning dish of the English kitchen: yesterday's potatoes and cabbage, pressed into a cake and fried in fat until a deep golden crust forms on both faces. The name is onomatopoeia, claimed with total confidence by every old source — the cabbage "bubbles" and the pan "squeaks" as the cake fries. It was born of absolute economy and survived into the era of plenty because it is, quietly, better than the sum of its parts: the potato binds, the cabbage chars sweet at the edges, and the crust — the whole point — is the best texture on any breakfast plate. This is the canonical master, the one every other bubble-and-squeak record on these sites derives from. The secrets are unglamorous and few: cold, dry, well-mashed potato; cabbage squeezed of its water; a heavy pan with a real layer of fat; and patience — the crust takes eight minutes a side and cannot be hurried.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

The base (yesterday's leftovers are ideal)

  • the quiet classic note

For frying

To serve

- **The potato must be cold and dry.** Warm, freshly boiled potato makes a gluey cake that steams instead of crusting. If you are cooking from scratch today, boil 700 g potatoes in salted water, drain, and steam-dry 5 minutes, then chill at least an hour — or spread them on a tray in the freezer for 20 minutes. - **Squeeze the cabbage.** Whether last night's or freshly cooked (blanched 3 minutes, shocked cold), wring it in a clean tea towel until it stops dripping. Wet cabbage is the number-one cause of a bubble that never crisps. - **Rough mash, not smooth.** A few small lumps are wanted; a food-processor purée makes paste. A fork and thirty seconds' effort is the correct tool.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • Mix: holds as a ragged cake when squeezed, seasoned bolder than tastes right.
  • Chilled 20 minutes; firm enough to lift clean.
  • First crust: 8 undisturbed minutes, deep gold, fish slice slides under with crisp resistance.
  • Second crust: matching gold; centre steaming hot throughout, at 75 °C for 30 seconds; audible crack under the knife.

Bubble and Squeak

Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 25 minutes · Total: 40 minutes · Serves 4 as a breakfast component

Ingredients

The base (yesterday's leftovers are ideal)

  • 500 g cold cooked floury potatoes (Maris Piper or King Edward), roughly mashed
  • 250 g cold cooked cabbage — spring cabbage, savoy, or pointed — or 200 g cabbage plus 100 g cooked Brussels sprouts
  • 30 g unsalted butter, plus extra for frying
  • 2 spring onions, finely sliced (30 g), or ½ a small onion (75 g), finely diced and softened in butter
  • 40 g mature Cheddar, grated (optional, and welcome)
  • 3 g fine sea salt
  • 1 g freshly cracked black pepper
  • A grating of nutmeg (about 0.5 g) — the quiet classic note

For frying

  • 30 ml / 28 g of the bacon's rendered fat, goose fat, or a 50/50 mix of butter and neutral oil

To serve

  • Fried or poached eggs, brown breakfast sauce, or the rest of the fry-up

Instructions

  1. **Mix and season the cake.** In a large bowl, combine the cold mash, squeezed cabbage, spring onion, butter, cheese (if using), salt, pepper, and nutmeg. Mix with a fork or your hands until it just holds together when squeezed — it should feel like a damp, clumpy dough, not a smooth purée. Taste and adjust the salt now; it must be seasoned a shade bolder than seems right, because the crust will mute it. Checkpoint — a fistful squeezed in your palm holds as a ragged cake that only just keeps shape. If it crumbles dry, work in 1–2 tablespoons of butter; if it is sticky-wet, the cabbage needs another squeeze.
  2. **Shape and chill.** Press the mixture into a round 3–4 cm deep in the bowl (or divide into 8 individual cakes, 130 g each, about 2 cm thick). Chill 20 minutes to firm — this is what lets it lift and flip in one piece. Checkpoint — the surface is firm to the touch and a palette knife slides under the edge of a test cake without smearing.
  3. **Fry the first crust — low, flat, and untouched.** Heat the fat in a 24 cm heavy non-stick or well-seasoned cast-iron pan over medium-low until it just foams. Slide in the whole cake (or the individual cakes, spaced) and press it flat with a spatula to 2–3 cm. Then leave it entirely alone for 8 minutes. The underside needs to build a continuous deep-golden crust, and every premature poke tears it. Checkpoint — at 8 minutes the cake's edges show deep gold creeping up their sides, the pan emits a low, steady sizzle (the "squeak"), and you can slide a fish slice fully under the cake in one confident pass, feeling crisp resistance — not soft stodge — against the metal.
  4. **Flip it like a professional.** Place a flat plate or board upside-down over the pan, invert the whole thing in one confident move, then slide the cake back into the pan, uncooked face down. Add a fresh knob of butter (10 g) around the edge for the second side. Cook another 6–8 minutes. Checkpoint — the second face matches the first — an even, deep golden-brown crust across the whole surface — and the cake's sides have lost their raw, pale look. Check the centre is steaming hot throughout; as a thermometer check, hold the centre at 75 °C for 30 seconds.
  5. **Rest one minute, then quarter and serve.** Slide the cake onto a board, let it sit a minute to set, then cut into wedges at the table or in the kitchen. The crust should crack audibly under the knife. Checkpoint — the eating test: the outside crunches, the inside is soft but not gluey, the cabbage shows caramelised dark edges, and the plate underneath carries a few golden crumbly bits — the bubble's signature debris.

Finish & Plate

The classic landing is bubble with fried eggs on top — the yolks run into the crust — and brown breakfast sauce on the side. On the full plate, it replaces or joins the hash browns, where its cabbage sweetness earns its seat. Serve the cakes straight away; leftovers used in the mix should be reheated only once.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Cake sticks and tears on the first flipPan not hot enough before it went in, or poked earlyFoam the fat properly first; hands off for the full 8 minutes
No crust, just pale fried mashWet cabbage, warm potato, or heat too low to frySqueeze the cabbage; chill everything; the fat should foam, not merely melt
Gluey, dense middleOverworked potato or over-mashedFork-mash roughly; lumps are texture, not error
Falls apart when cutToo little binder or no chillAdd the egg-free binder of 1 tbsp butter pressed through, and the full 20-minute chill
Burnt crust, cold middleHeat too highMedium-low, always; the slow crust is the recipe

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **Storage:** Refrigerate the cake mix and use it within 2 days of originally cooking its ingredients, or freeze shaped cakes (interleaved with paper) for up to 2 months. Reheat the cakes until steaming hot throughout and serve straight away; do not reheat them again. - **Variation — bubble and squeak with fried eggs:** the canonical pairing, its own record: cakes shaped individual-size, two eggs fried in the same pan's fat after. - **Variation — sprout and bacon bubble:** 150 g cooked Brussels and 100 g cooked chopped bacon folded in; a Christmas-morning institution. - **Variation — colcannon-adjacent, soft:** for the mash-and-greens version without the crust, stir-fry only 5 minutes, soft and buttery, no flip — the Irish cousin, equally at home under a poached egg. - **The economy note:** the whole point is using what exists — any cold cooked greens, any roast potato (crushed, not mashed), a spoon of leftover pan fat. The recipe above is the standard; the dish invites deviation.
